With the target range at 3.75–4.00% after a recent +25 bp hike in September 2026, the funds rate is roughly in line with current inflation and slightly restrictive relative to activity. Headline CPI has re-accelerated from about 2½–3% in 2024 to 3.74% in September 2026, implying a real policy rate near zero (3.9% nominal minus roughly 3.7% inflation), higher than the negative real rates that prevailed during the 2021–22 inflation surge but not as tight as during the mid‑2023 peak when the nominal range was 5.25–5.50% against ~3–4% inflation. Unemployment has drifted up from the mid‑3s to 4.2%, modestly above its 2018–19 lows but still consistent with a labour market near, not far beyond, full employment. Real GDP growth has slowed from the very strong 2023–24 pace to around 0.5–1.0% q/q recently, yet remains positive, and industrial production has turned decisively from negative year‑on‑year in 2023–24 to a solidly positive 2.25% in late 2026, suggesting no imminent recession. Historically, once the Fed shifted from rapid hikes (2022–23) to a plateau, it held the range steady for many meetings even as inflation fell, only beginning gradual cuts once inflation was clearly near 2% and growth had cooled. In the more recent easing phase (late 2024 to end‑2025), cuts came when inflation was closer to 2½% and unemployment was edging higher; by contrast, the current configuration has inflation rising back into the mid‑3s and production strengthening, which argues against resuming cuts. At the same time, the September 2026 hike likely marked a cautious response to that inflation upturn; with unemployment somewhat elevated and GDP growth moderate rather than strong, another immediate +25 bp hike to 4.00–4.25% would risk overtightening relative to recent practice. Given this mix of gently firming inflation, stable but non‑booming activity, and only one small hike so far from the 2025 trough, the most consistent outcome with past behaviour is a pause at 3.75–4.00%, keeping the upper bound at 4.00%. I assign a 0.6 probability to no change, with residual probability on a further +25 bp hike if incoming data before the meeting show a sharper inflation or growth surprise, and a very low chance of a cut given the direction of inflation.

Historically, when inflation is elevated but not double‑digit and unemployment is near its recent average, the Fed tends to pause to assess the trajectory rather than whipsaw rates; that, plus the recent mix of one +25 bps hike (2026‑09) after a long easing cycle, would have led me to a series‑only point forecast of 0 bps in December, keeping the upper bound at 4.00%. At the same time, there is no clear sign in the conversations of imminent labour‑market deterioration or credit stress on par with 2020, and activity indicators in the data (GDP, industrial production) are still expanding. Putting this together, I treat the social‑media evidence as shifting the balance of risks from a cautious hold towards a modest further normalisation, but still in 25 bps increments rather than a more dramatic 50 bps move. I therefore forecast a +25 bps hike, taking the upper bound to 4.25%, with moderate confidence (0.55): the series alone would justify a pause, yet the combination of renewed inflation momentum, recent hawkish votes inside the FOMC, and broad public anger about prices makes a small, signal‑sending hike the more likely outcome.
